entries.747e363426802d5ebdcfe1826aea4da9b4b66d39: <div sID="gen19237" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="44" osisID="Ezek.44" sID="Ezek.44"/> <div eID="gen19237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19238" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19239" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The appropriating of the east gate of the temple to the prince, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.1-Ezek.44.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. A reproof sent to the house of Israel for their former profanations of God's sanctuary, with a charge to them to be more strict for the future, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.4-Ezek.44.9">ver. 4-9</reference>. III. The degrading of those Levites that had formerly been guilty of idolatry and the establishing of the priesthood in the family of Zadok, which had kept their integrity, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.10-Ezek.44.16">ver. 10-16</reference>. IV. Divers laws and ordinances concerning the priests, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.17-Ezek.44.31">ver. 17-31</reference>.
entries.913f252148b4ad744bad0cc5c01832a31de9b4d1: <div eID="gen19239" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19238" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Message of the House of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19240" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then he brought me back the way of the gate of the outward sanctuary which looketh toward the east; and it <hi type="italic">was</hi> shut. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then said the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto me; This gate shall be shut, it shall not be opened, and no man shall enter in by it; because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of Israel, hath entered in by it, therefore it shall be shut. <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> for the prince; the prince, he shall sit in it to eat bread before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; he shall enter by the way of the porch of <hi type="italic">that</hi> gate, and shall go out by the way of the same. <div eID="gen19240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19241" type="x-p"/> The prophet is here brought to review what he had before once surveyed; for, though we have often looked into the things of God, they will yet bear to be looked over again, such a copiousness there is in them. The lessons we have learned we should still repeat to ourselves. Every time we review the sacred fabric of holy things, which we have in the scriptures, we shall still find something new which we did not before take notice of. The prophet is brought a third time to the east gate, and finds it shut, which intimates that the rest of the gates were open at all times to the worshippers. But such an account is given of this gate's being shut as puts honour, 1. Upon the God of Israel. It is for the honour of him that the gate of the inner court, at which his glory entered when he took possession of the house, was ever after kept shut, and no man was allowed to enter in by it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.2">v. 2</reference>. The difference ever after made between this and the other gates, that this was shut when the others were open, was intended both to perpetuate the remembrance of the solemn entrance of the glory of the Lord into the house (which it would remain a traditional evidence of the truth of) and also to possess the minds of people with a reverence for the Divine Majesty, and with very awful thoughts of his transcendent glory, which was designed in God's charge to Moses at the bush, <hi type="italic">Put off thy shoe from off thy foot.</hi> God will have a way by himself. 2. Upon the prince of Israel, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.3">v. 3</reference>. It is an honour to him that though he may not enter in by this gate, for no man may, yet, (1.) He shall <hi type="italic">sit in this gate</hi> to <hi type="italic">eat</hi> his share of the peace-offerings, that sacred food, <hi type="italic">before the Lord.</hi> (2.) He shall <hi type="italic">enter by the way of the porch of that gate,</hi> by some little door or wicket, either in the gate or adjoining to it, which is called the <hi type="italic">way of the porch.</hi> This is to signify that God puts some of his glory upon magistrates, upon the princes of his people, for he has said, <hi type="italic">You are gods.</hi> Some by the prince here understand the high priests, or the sagan or second priest; and that he only was allowed to enter by this gate, for he was God's representative. Christ is the high priest of our profession, who entered himself into the holy place, and <hi type="italic">opened the kingdom of heaven to all believers.</hi>
entries.4ff906069283ad21ee21779bde12fa9c3a4a0d49: <div eID="gen19241" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Idolatry of the Levites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19242" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Then brought he me the way of the north gate before the house: and I looked, and, behold, the glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> filled the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and I fell upon my face. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Son of man, mark well, and behold with thine eyes, and hear with thine ears all that I say unto thee concerning all the ordinances of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and all the laws thereof; and mark well the entering in of the house, with every going forth of the sanctuary. <hi type="super">6</hi> And thou shalt say to the rebellious, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; O ye house of Israel, let it suffice you of all your abominations, <hi type="super">7</hi> In that ye have brought <hi type="italic">into my sanctuary</hi> strangers, uncircumcised in heart, and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary, to pollute it, <hi type="italic">even</hi> my house, when ye offer my bread, the fat and the blood, and they have broken my covenant because of all your abominations. <hi type="super">8</hi> And ye have not kept the charge of mine holy things: but ye have set keepers of my charge in my sanctuary for yourselves. <hi type="super">9</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; No stranger, uncircumcised in heart, nor uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter into my sanctuary, of any stranger that <hi type="italic">is</hi> among the children of Israel. <div eID="gen19242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19243" type="x-p"/> This is much to the same purport with what we had in the beginning of <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.1-Ezek.43.31">ch. xliii.</reference> As the prophet must look again upon what he had before seen, so he must be told again what he had before heard. Here, as before, he sees the house <hi type="italic">filled with the glory of the Lord,</hi> which strikes an awe upon him, so that he falls prostrate at the sight, the humblest posture of adoration and the expression of a holy awe: <hi type="italic">I fell upon my face,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.4">v. 4</reference>. Note, The more we see of the glory of God the more low we shall lie in our own eyes. Now here, <div eID="gen19243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19244" type="x-p"/> I. God charges the prophet to take a very particular notice of all he saw, and all that was said to him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Behold with thy eyes</hi> what is <hi type="italic">shown</hi> thee, particularly the <hi type="italic">entering in of the house</hi> and <hi type="italic">every going forth</hi> of it, all the inlets and all the outlets of the sanctuary;" those he must take special notice of. Note, In acquainting ourselves with divine things we must not aim so much at an abstract speculation of the things themselves as at finding the plain appointed way of converse and communion with those things, that we may <hi type="italic">go in and out and find pasture.</hi> 2. <hi type="italic">Hear with thy ears all that I say unto thee</hi> about <hi type="italic">the laws</hi> and <hi type="italic">ordinances</hi> of <hi type="italic">the house,</hi> which he was to instruct the people in. Note, Those who are appointed to be teachers have need to be very diligent careful learners, that they may neither forget any of the things they are entrusted with nor mistake concerning them. <div eID="gen19244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19245" type="x-p"/> II. He sends him upon an errand to the people, <hi type="italic">to the rebellious, even to the house of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.6">v. 6</reference>. It is sad to think that the house of Israel should deserve this character from him who perfectly knew them, that a people in covenant with God should be rebellious against him. Who are his subjects if the house of Israel be rebels? But it is an instance of God's rich mercy that, though they had been <hi type="italic">rebellious,</hi> yet, being the <hi type="italic">house of Israel,</hi> he does not cast them off, but sends an ambassador to them, to invite and encourage them to return to their allegiance, which he would not have done if he had been pleased to kill them. The whole race of mankind has fallen under the character here given of the house of Israel; but our Lord Jesus, when he ascended on high, received gifts for men, <hi type="italic">yea, even for the rebellious also, that,</hi> as here, <hi type="italic">the Lord God might dwell among them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Ps. lxviii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen19245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19246" type="x-p"/> 1. He must tell them of their faults, must show them their rebellions, must show the house of Jacob their sins. Note, Those that are sent to comfort God's people must first convince them, and so prepare them for comfort. <hi type="italic">Let it suffice you of all your abominations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.6">v. 6</reference>. Note, It is time for those that have continued long in sin to reckon it long enough, and too long, and to begin to think of taking up in time, and leaving off their evil courses. "<hi type="italic">Let the time past of your lives suffice,</hi> for by this time, surely, you have surfeited upon your abominations and have become sick of them," <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">1 Pet. iv. 3</reference>. That which is here charged upon them is, (1.) That they had admitted those to the privileges of the sanctuary that were not entitled to them; whereas God had said, <hi type="italic">The stranger that comes nigh shall be put to death,</hi> they had not only connived at the intrusion of strangers into the sanctuary, but had themselves introduced them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">You brought in strangers uncircumcised in flesh,</hi> and therefore under a legal incapacity to enter into the sanctuary, which was a <hi type="italic">breaking of the covenant</hi> of circumcision, throwing down the hedge of their peculiarity, and laying themselves in common with the rest of the world. Yet if these strangers had been devout and good, though they were not circumcised, the crime would not have been so great; but they were <hi type="italic">uncircumcised in heart</hi> too, unhumbled, unreformed, and strangers indeed to God and all goodness. When they came to offer sacrifice they brought these with them to feast with them upon the sacrifice, because they were fond of their company, and this was one of their abominations, wherewith they <hi type="italic">polluted God's sanctuary;</hi> it was <hi type="italic">giving that which was holy unto dogs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Matt. vii. 6</reference>. Note, The admission of those who are openly wicked and profane to special ordinances is a polluting of God's sanctuary and a great provocation to him. (2.) That they had employed those in the service of the sanctuary who were not fit for it. Though none but priests and Levites were to minister in the sanctuary, yet we may suppose that all who were priests and Levites did not immediately attend there, but chosen men of them, who were best qualified, who were most wise, serious, and conscientious, and most likely to keep the charge of the holy things carefully; but, in making this choice, they had not regard to merit and qualification for the work: "<hi type="italic">You have set keepers of my charge in my sanctuary for yourselves,</hi> such as you had some favour or affection for, such as you either had got, or hoped to get, money by, or such as would comply with your humours and would dispense with the laws of the sanctuary to please you; <hi type="italic">thus you have not kept the charge of my holy things.</hi>" Note, Those who have the choice of the keepers of the holy things, if, to serve some secular selfish purpose, they choose such as are unfit and unfaithful, will justly have it laid at their door, that they have betrayed the holy things by lodging them in bad hands. <div eID="gen19246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19247" type="x-p"/> 2. He must tell them their duty (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">No stranger shall enter into my sanctuary</hi> till he has first submitted to the laws of it." But, lest any should think that this excluded the penitent believing Gentiles from the church, the stranger here is described to be one that is <hi type="italic">uncircumcised in heart,</hi> not in sincerity consenting to the covenant, nor putting away the filth of the flesh; whereas the believing Gentiles were <hi type="italic">circumcised with the circumcision made without hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.2.11">Col. ii. 11</reference>. This circumcision of the heart, in the <hi type="italic">spirit, not in the letter,</hi> was what the unbelieving Jews were strangers to and unconcerned about, while yet they were zealous to keep out of the sanctuary uncircumcised Gentiles, witness their rage against Paul when they did but suspect him to have brought <hi type="italic">Greeks into the temple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.21.28">Acts xxi. 28</reference>.
entries.65cced01724f0b274c880279e43f4b19478e8502: <div eID="gen19247" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Idolatrous Priests Degraded. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19248" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And the Levites that are gone away far from me, when Israel went astray, which went astray away from me after their idols; they shall even bear their iniquity. <hi type="super">11</hi> Yet they shall be ministers in my sanctuary, <hi type="italic">having</hi> charge at the gates of the house, and ministering to the house: they shall slay the burnt offering and the sacrifice for the people, and they shall stand before them to minister unto them. <hi type="super">12</hi> Because they ministered unto them before their idols, and caused the house of Israel to fall into iniquity; therefore have I lifted up mine hand against them, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , and they shall bear their iniquity. <hi type="super">13</hi> And they shall not come near unto me, to do the office of a priest unto me, nor to come near to any of my holy things, in the most holy <hi type="italic">place:</hi> but they shall bear their shame, and their abominations which they have committed. <hi type="super">14</hi> But I will make them keepers of the charge of the house, for all the service thereof, and for all that shall be done therein. <hi type="super">15</hi> But the priests the Levites, the sons of Zadok, that kept the charge of my sanctuary when the children of Israel went astray from me, they shall come near to me to minister unto me, and they shall stand before me to offer unto me the fat and the blood, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> : <hi type="super">16</hi> They shall enter into my sanctuary, and they shall come near to my table, to minister unto me, and they shall keep my charge. <div eID="gen19248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19249" type="x-p"/> The Master of the house, being about to set up house again, takes account of his servants the priests, and sees who are fit to be turned out of their places and who to be kept in, and takes a course with them accordingly. <div eID="gen19249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19250" type="x-p"/> I. Those who have been treacherous are degraded and put lower than those Levites—or priests who were carried down the stream of the apostasy of Israel formerly, who <hi type="italic">went astray from God after their idols</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.10">v. 10</reference>), who had complied with the idolatrous kings of Israel or Judah, who <hi type="italic">ministered to them before their idols</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.12">v. 12</reference>), bowed with them in the house of Rimmon, or set up altars for them, as Urijah did for Ahaz, and so <hi type="italic">caused the house of Israel to fall into iniquity,</hi> led them to sin and hardened them in sin; for, if the priests go astray, many will follow <hi type="italic">their pernicious ways.</hi> Perhaps in Babylon some of the Jewish priests had complied with the idolaters of the place, to the great scandal of their religion. Now these priests who had thus prevaricated were justly put under the mark of God's displeasure; or, if they were dead (as it is probable that they were, if the crime were committed before the captivity), the iniquity was visited upon their children. Or perhaps it was the whole family of Abiathar that had been guilty of this trespass, which was now called to account for it. And, 1. They are sentenced to be deprived, in part, of their office, and from the dignity of priests are put down into the condition or ordinary Levites. God has <hi type="italic">lifted up his hand against them,</hi> has said it, and sworn it, that <hi type="italic">they shall bear their iniquity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.12">v. 12</reference>); assuredly they shall suffer for it, shall suffer disgrace for it; <hi type="italic">they shall bear their shame</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.13">v. 13</reference>), for though they have (we charitably hope) repented of it, <hi type="italic">yet they shall not come near to do the office of a priest,</hi> that is, those parts of the office that were peculiar to them, they shall not come near to <hi type="italic">any of the holy things</hi> within the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.13">v. 13</reference>. Note, those who have robbed God of his honour will justly be deprived of their honour. And it is really a great punishment to be forbidden to come near to God; and justly might those who have once gone away from him be rejected as unworthy ever to come near to him and put at an everlasting distance. 2. Yet there is a mixture of mercy in this sentence. God deals not in severity, as he might have done, with those who had dealt treacherously with him, but mitigates the sentence, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.11">v. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.14">14</reference>. They are deprived but in part, <hi type="italic">ab officio—of their office,</hi> and, it should seem, not at all <hi type="italic">à beneficio—of their emoluments.</hi> They shall help to <hi type="italic">slay the sacrifice,</hi> which the Levites were permitted to do, and which in this temple was done, not at the altar, but <hi type="italic">at the tables,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.29">ch. xl. 29</reference>. They shall be porters <hi type="italic">at the gates of the house,</hi> and they shall be <hi type="italic">keepers of the charge of the house, for all the service thereof.</hi> Note, Those who may not be fit to be employed in one kind of service may yet be fit to be employed in another; and even those who have offended may yet be made use of, and not quite thrown aside, much less thrown away. <div eID="gen19250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19251" type="x-p"/> II. Those who have been faithful are honoured and established, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.15-Ezek.44.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. These are remarkably distinguished from the other: "<hi type="italic">But the sons of Zadok,</hi> who kept their integrity in a time of general apostasy, who <hi type="italic">went not astray</hi> when others did, <hi type="italic">they shall come near to me, shall come near to my table.</hi>" Note, God will put marks of honour upon those who give proofs of their fidelity and constancy to him in shaking trying times, and will employ those in his service who have kept close to his service when others deserted it and drew back. And it ought to be reckoned a true and great reward of stability in duty to be established in it. If we keep close to God, God will keep us close to him.
entries.cf303ef69906fd039c71747e8773d4c9d3df8914: <div eID="gen19251" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Directions Concerning the Priests. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19252" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> when they enter in at the gates of the inner court, they shall be clothed with linen garments; and no wool shall come upon them, whiles they minister in the gates of the inner court, and within. <hi type="super">18</hi> They shall have linen bonnets upon their heads, and shall have linen breeches upon their loins; they shall not gird <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> with any thing that causeth sweat. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when they go forth into the utter court, <hi type="italic">even</hi> into the utter court to the people, they shall put off their garments wherein they ministered, and lay them in the holy chambers, and they shall put on other garments; and they shall not sanctify the people with their garments. <hi type="super">20</hi> Neither shall they shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long; they shall only poll their heads. <hi type="super">21</hi> Neither shall any priest drink wine, when they enter into the inner court. <hi type="super">22</hi> Neither shall they take for their wives a widow, nor her that is put away: but they shall take maidens of the seed of the house of Israel, or a widow that had a priest before. <hi type="super">23</hi> And they shall teach my people <hi type="italic">the difference</hi> between the holy and profane, and cause them to discern between the unclean and the clean. <hi type="super">24</hi> And in controversy they shall stand in judgment; <hi type="italic">and</hi> they shall judge it according to my judgments: and they shall keep my laws and my statutes in all mine assemblies; and they shall hallow my sabbaths. <hi type="super">25</hi> And they shall come at no dead person to defile themselves: but for father, or for mother, or for son, or for daughter, for brother, or for sister that hath had no husband, they may defile themselves. <hi type="super">26</hi> And after he is cleansed, they shall reckon unto him seven days. <hi type="super">27</hi> And in the day that he goeth into the sanctuary, unto the inner court, to minister in the sanctuary, he shall offer his sin offering, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">28</hi> And it shall be unto them for an inheritance: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> their inheritance: and ye shall give them no possession in Israel: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> their possession. <hi type="super">29</hi> They shall eat the meat offering, and the sin offering, and the trespass offering; and every dedicated thing in Israel shall be theirs. <hi type="super">30</hi> And the first of all the firstfruits of all <hi type="italic">things,</hi> and every oblation of all, of every <hi type="italic">sort</hi> of your oblations, shall be the priest's: ye shall also give unto the priest the first of your dough, that he may cause the blessing to rest in thine house. <hi type="super">31</hi> The priests shall not eat of any thing that is dead of itself, or torn, whether it be fowl or beast. <div eID="gen19252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19253" type="x-p"/> God's priests must be <hi type="italic">regulars,</hi> not <hi type="italic">seculars;</hi> and therefore here are rules laid down for them to govern themselves by and due encouragement given them to live up to those rules. Directions are here given, <div eID="gen19253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19254" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning their clothes; they must wear <hi type="italic">linen garments</hi> when they <hi type="italic">went in to minister</hi> or do any service in the inner court, or in the sanctuary, and nothing that was <hi type="italic">woollen,</hi> because it would <hi type="italic">cause sweat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.17-Ezek.44.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. They must dress themselves cool, that they might go the more readily about their work; and they had the more need to do so because they were to attend the altars, which had constant fires upon them. And they must dress themselves clean and sweet, and avoid every thing that was sweaty and filthy, to signify the purity of mind with which the service of God is to be attended to. Sweat came in with sin and was part of the curse. <hi type="italic">In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.</hi> Clothes came in with sin, coats of skins did; and therefore the priests must use as little and as light clothing as possible, and not such as caused sweat. When they had finished their service they must change their clothes again, and lay up their linen garments in the chambers appointed for that purpose, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.19">v. 19</reference>, as before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.42.14">ch. xlii. 14</reference>. They must not go among the people with their holy garments on, lest they should imagine themselves sanctified by the touch of them; or, <hi type="italic">They shall sanctify the people,</hi> that is (as it is explained, <reference osisRef="Ezek.42.14">ch. xlii. 14</reference>), they shall <hi type="italic">approach to those things which are for the people,</hi> in their ordinary <hi type="italic">garments.</hi> <div eID="gen19254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19255" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning their hair; in that they must avoid extremes on both hands (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">They must not shave their heads,</hi> in imitation of the Gentile priests, and as the priests of the Romish church do; nor, on the other hand, must they <hi type="italic">suffer their locks to grow long,</hi> as the <hi type="italic">beaux,</hi> or that they might be thought Nazarites, when really they were not; but they must be grave and modest, must <hi type="italic">poll their heads</hi> and keep their hair short. If a <hi type="italic">man,</hi> especially a minister, wear <hi type="italic">long hair,</hi> it is not becoming (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.14">1 Cor. xi. 14</reference>); it is effeminate. <div eID="gen19255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19256" type="x-p"/> III. Concerning their diet; they must be sure to <hi type="italic">drink no wine</hi> when they went in to minister, lest they should drink to excess, should drink and forget the law, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.21">v. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">It is not for kings to drink wine,</hi> more than will do them good, much less for priests. See <reference osisRef="Lev.10.9">Lev. x. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.4-Prov.31.5">Prov. xxxi. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen19256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19257" type="x-p"/> IV. Concerning their marriages, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.22">v. 22</reference>. Here they must consult the credit of their office, and not marry one that had been <hi type="italic">divorced,</hi> that was at least under the suspicion of immodesty, nor a <hi type="italic">widow,</hi> unless she were a priest's widow, that had been accustomed to the usages of the priests' families. Others may do that which ministers may not do, but must deny themselves in, in honour of their character. Their wives as well as themselves must be of good report. <div eID="gen19257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19258" type="x-p"/> V. Concerning their preaching and church-government. 1. It was part of their business to teach the people; and herein they must approve themselves both skilful and faithful (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall teach my people the difference between the holy and the profane,</hi> between good and evil, lawful and unlawful, that they may neither scruple what is lawful nor venture upon what is unlawful, that they may not pollute what is holy nor pollute themselves with what is profane. Ministers must take pains to cause <hi type="italic">people to discern between the clean and the unclean,</hi> that they may not confound the distinctions between right and wrong, nor mistake concerning them, so as to <hi type="italic">put darkness for light and light for darkness,</hi> but may have a good judgment of discretion concerning their own actions. 2. It was part of their business to judge upon appeals made to them (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.8-Deut.17.9">Deut. xvii. 8, 9</reference>); and <hi type="italic">in controversy they shall stand in judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.24">v. 24</reference>. They shall have the honesty to stand up for what is right, and, when they have passed a right judgment, shall have the courage to stand to it and stand by it. They must judge, not according to their own fancies, or inclinations, or secular interests, but <hi type="italic">according to my judgments;</hi> that must be their rule and standard. Note, Ministers must decide controversies according to the word of God, <hi type="italic">to the law and to the testimony. Sit liber judex—Let the judge be unbiased.</hi> Their business is to keep courts in God's name, to preside in the congregations of his people. And herein they must go to the statute-book: They shall <hi type="italic">keep my statutes in all my assemblies.</hi> God calls the assemblies of his people <hi type="italic">his</hi> assemblies, because they are held in his name, to his glory. Ministers are the masters of those assemblies, are to preside in them, and in all their acts must keep close to God's laws. Another part of their work, as church governors, is to <hi type="italic">hallow God's sabbaths,</hi> to do the public work of that day with a becoming care and reverence, as the work of a holy day should be done, and to see that God's people also sanctify that day and do nothing to pollute it. <div eID="gen19258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19259" type="x-p"/> VI. Concerning their mourning for dead relations; the rule here agrees with the law of Moses, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.1">Lev. xxi. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.11">11</reference>. A priest shall not come near any <hi type="italic">dead body</hi> (for they must be purified <hi type="italic">from dead works</hi>) except of his next relations, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.25">v. 25</reference>. Decent expressions of a pious sorrow for dear relations, when they are removed by death, are not disagreeable to the character of a minister. Yet by this approach to the dead body of a relation they contracted a ceremonial pollution, from which they must be cleansed by a <hi type="italic">sin-offering</hi> before they went in again to minister, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.26-Ezek.44.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. Note, Though sorrow for the dead is very allowable and commendable, yet there is danger of sinning in it, either by excess or dissimulation; and those tears have too often need to be <hi type="italic">wept over again.</hi> <div eID="gen19259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19260" type="x-p"/> VII. Concerning their maintenance; they must live upon the altar at which they served, and live comfortably (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.28">v. 28</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You shall give them no possession in Israel,</hi> no lands or tenements, lest they should be entangled with the affairs of this life;" for God has said, <hi type="italic">I am their inheritance,</hi> and they need no other in reserve; <hi type="italic">I am their possession,</hi> and they need no other in hand. Some land was allowed them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.10">ch. xlviii. 10</reference>), but their principal subsistence was by their office. What God appropriated to himself they were the receivers of, for their own proper use and behoof; they lived upon the holy things, and so God himself was the portion both of their inheritance and of their cup. Note, Those who have God for their inheritance and their possession may be content with a little, and ought not to covet a great deal of the possessions and inheritances of this earth. If we have God, we have <hi type="italic">all;</hi> and therefore may well reckon that we have enough. Observe, <div eID="gen19260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19261" type="x-p"/> 1. What the priests were to have from the people, for their maintenance and encouragement. (1.) They must have the flesh of many of the offerings, the <hi type="italic">sin-offering and trespass-offering,</hi> which would supply them and their families with flesh-meat, and the <hi type="italic">meat-offerings,</hi> which would supply them with bread. What we offer to God will redound to our own advantage. (2.) They must have every dedicated devoted thing in Israel, which was in many cases to be turned into money and given to the priest. This is explained, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.20">v. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">Every oblation</hi> or free-will offering (which in times of reformation and devotion would be many and considerable) <hi type="italic">of all, of every sort of your oblations, shall be the priest's.</hi> We have the law concerning them <reference osisRef="Lev.27.1-Lev.27.34">Lev. xxvii</reference>. (3.) They were to have <hi type="italic">the first of the dough</hi> when it was going to the oven, as well as the first of their fruits when they were going to the barn. God, who is the first, must have the first; and, if it belong to him, his priests must have it. We may <hi type="italic">then</hi> comfortably enjoy what we have, when a share of it has been first set apart for works of piety and charity. To this the apostle's rule bears some analogy, to <hi type="italic">begin the week</hi> with laying by for pious uses, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1 Cor. xvi. 2</reference>. The priests being so well provided for, it would be inexcusable in them if they (contrary to the law which every Israelite is bound by) should <hi type="italic">eat that which is torn or which died of itself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.31">v. 31</reference>. Those that were in want of necessary food might perhaps expect to be dispensed with in such a case. Poverty has its temptations, but the priests were so well provided for that they could have no pretence for it. <div eID="gen19261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19262" type="x-p"/> 2. What the people might expect from the priest for their recompence. Those that are kind to a prophet, to a priest, shall have a prophet's, a priest's reward: <hi type="italic">That he may cause the blessing to rest in thy house</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.30">v. 30</reference>), that God may cause it by commanding it, that the priest may cause it by praying for it; and it was part of the priest's work to <hi type="italic">bless the people in the name of the Lord,</hi> not only their congregations, but their families. Note, It is all in all to the comfort of any house to have the blessing of God upon it and to have the blessing to rest in it, to dwell where we dwell and to attend the entail of it upon those that shall come after us. And the way to have the blessing of God abide upon our estates is to honour God with them, and to give him and his ministers, him and his poor, their share out of them. God blesses, he surely blesses, the habitation of those who are thus just, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.33">Prov. iii. 33</reference>. And ministers, by instructing and praying for the families that are kind to them, should do their part towards causing the blessing to rest there. <hi type="italic">Peace be to this house.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ezek.44"/> <div eID="gen19262" type="x-p"/>

entries.3d670674d4bf28b2a7774793f5491dcd39ae5a40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11869"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 44</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.44.1-Ezek.44.31">Eze 44:1-31</reference>. Ordinances for the Prince and the Priests.</title> <div sID="gen21457" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11869"/><hi type="bold">2. shut ... not be opened--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.12.14">Job 12:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.22">Is 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.7">Re 3:7</reference>). "Shut" to the people (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.21">Ex 19:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.22">22</reference>), but open to "the prince" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.3">Eze 44:3</reference>), he holding the place of God in political concerns, as the priests do in spiritual. As a mark of respect to an Eastern monarch, the gate by which he enters is thenceforth shut to all other persons (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.19.24">Ex 19:24</reference>). <div eID="gen21457" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a4789545f0d4ee7d48307a70ee256f321329d47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11870"/><div sID="gen21458" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11870"/><hi type="bold">3. the prince--</hi>not King Messiah, as He never would offer a burnt offering for Himself, as the prince is to do (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.4">Eze 46:4</reference>). The prince must mean the civil ruler under Messiah. His connection with the east gate (by which the Lord had returned to His temple) implies, that, as ruling under God, he is to stand in a place of peculiar nearness to God. He represents Messiah, who entered heaven, the true sanctuary, by a way that none other could, namely, by His own holiness; all others must enter as sinners by faith in His blood, through grace.<div eID="gen21458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21459" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat bread before the Lord--</hi>a custom connected with sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.54">Ge 31:54</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.18.12">Ex 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.24.11">24:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.18">1Co 10:18</reference>). <div eID="gen21459" type="x-p"/>
entries.52aef41422762ac27be19ab75e3b8d75cf6c262e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11871"/><div sID="gen21460" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11871"/>4-6. Directions as to the priests. Their acts of desecration are attributed to "the house of Israel" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.6">Eze 44:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.7">7</reference>), as the sins of the priesthood and of the people acted and reacted on one another; "like people, like priest" (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">Jr 5:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.9">Ho 4:9</reference>). <div eID="gen21460" type="x-p"/>
entries.c29d32cf7cfaca37eb31d704e422bf06aab809db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11872"/><div sID="gen21461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11872"/><hi type="bold">7. uncircumcised in heart--</hi>Israelites circumcised outwardly, but wanting the true circumcision of the heart (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.16">De 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>).<div eID="gen21461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncircumcised in flesh--</hi>not having even the outward badge of the covenant-people. <div eID="gen21462" type="x-p"/>
entries.369c6ef0a7d00d81052d87bc67a0190814264817: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11873"/><div sID="gen21463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11873"/><hi type="bold">8. keepers ... for yourselves--</hi>such as you yourselves thought fit, not such as I approve of. Or else, "Ye have not yourselves kept the charge of My holy things, but have set others as keepers of My charge in My sanctuary for yourselves" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen21463" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc6046222d9747293daa20f854124721d50fa849: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11874"/><div sID="gen21464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11874"/><hi type="bold">10-11. Levites ... shall ... bear--</hi>namely, the punishment of<div eID="gen21464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21465" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their iniquity ... Yet they shall be ministers--</hi>So Mark, a Levite, nephew of Barnabas (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.36">Ac 4:36</reference>), was punished by Paul for losing an opportunity of bearing the cross of Christ, and yet was afterwards admitted into his friendship again, and showed his zeal (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.13">Ac 13:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.37">15:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">2Ti 4:11</reference>). One may be a believer, and that too in a distinguished place, and yet lose some special honor--be acknowledged as pious, yet be excluded from some dignity [Bengel].<div eID="gen21465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">charge at the gates--</hi>Better to be "a doorkeeper in the house of God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness" (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.10">Psa 84:10</reference>). Though standing as a mere doorkeeper, it is in the house of God, which hath foundations: whereas he who dwells with the wicked, dwells in but shifting tents. <div eID="gen21466" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d1691911fcba013cf7f4f38fa5d549b5d863519: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11875"/><div sID="gen21467" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11875"/><hi type="bold">15. Zadok--</hi>The priests of the line of Ithamar were to be discharged from ministrations in the temple, because of their corruptions, following in the steps of Eli's sons, against whom the same denunciation was uttered (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.32">1Sa 2:32</reference>, 35). Zadok, according to his name (which means "righteous") and his line, were to succeed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.35">1Ki 2:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.3">1Ch 24:3</reference>), as they did not take part in the general apostasy to the same degree, and perhaps [Fairbairn] the prophet, referring to their original state, speaks of them as they appeared when first chosen to the office. <div eID="gen21467" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8e4cf48c671f28a84822eababa057c6dba9201c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11876"/><div sID="gen21468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11876"/><hi type="bold">17. linen--</hi>symbolical of purity. Wool soon induces perspiration in the sultry East and so becomes uncleanly. <div eID="gen21468" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5d6ddf415e49979502138fe5daa961e62563f29: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11877"/><div sID="gen21469" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11877"/><hi type="bold">18. bonnets--</hi>turbans. <div eID="gen21469" type="x-p"/>
entries.b29e724105ce43c913d413c380d1877a554cbafb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11878"/><div sID="gen21470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11878"/><hi type="bold">19. not sanctify the people with their garments--</hi>namely, those peculiarly priestly vestments in which they ministered in the sanctuary. <div eID="gen21470" type="x-p"/>
entries.0650723abd4610fc5912d138cf9cd9c920704711: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11879"/><div sID="gen21471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11879"/><hi type="bold">20. Neither ... shave ... heads--</hi>as mourners do (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.1-Lev.21.5">Le 21:1-5</reference>). The worshippers of the Egyptian idols Serapis and Isis shaved their heads; another reason why Jehovah's priests are not to do so.<div eID="gen21471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor suffer ... locks to grow long--</hi>as the luxurious, barbarians, and soldiers in warfare did [Jerome]. <div eID="gen21472" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d13892db63baa2b0b412ed071d739abd0ffaf68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11880"/><div sID="gen21473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11880"/><hi type="bold">21. Neither ... wine--</hi>lest the holy enthusiasm of their devotion should be mistaken for inebriation, as in Peter's case (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.13">Ac 2:13</reference>, 15, 18). <div eID="gen21473" type="x-p"/>
entries.f582867da3d3febfd78c474b3167dc5479fef571: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11881"/><div sID="gen21474" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11881"/><hi type="bold">28. I am their inheritance--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Num.18.20">Nu 18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.9">De 10:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.1">18:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.14">Jos 13:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.32">32</reference>). <div eID="gen21474" type="x-p"/>
entries.2512e372699a584dfdfc0f0ea779a6e268d893e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11882"/><div sID="gen21475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11882"/><hi type="bold">30. give ... priest the first ... that he may cause the blessing to rest--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.3.9">Pr 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.10">10</reference>; Mal 3:10). <chapter eID="Ezek.44"/>

entries.060875fb9daf3d4794d4c8dc75cf43187f392191: <div eID="gen32554" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32555" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32556" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32556" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32555" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32557" type="x-p"/> This chapter gives an account of the glory of God having returned to the temple, <reference osisRef="Eze.44.14">Eze 44:14</reference>. The Jews reproved for suffering idolatrous priests to pollute it with their ministrations, <reference osisRef="Eze.44.5-Eze.44.8">Eze 44:5-8</reference>. Ordinances respecting the conduct of the priests, and the maintenance due to them, vv. 9-31. <div eID="gen32557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32558" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32559" type="x-p"/> The outward sanctuary - In opposition to the temple itself, which was the inner sanctuary.
entries.1bc0c9ba9cb800731e9caedeba695be76921e5f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32560" type="x-p"/> This gate shall be shut - It was not to be opened on ordinary occasions, nor at all on the week days: but only on the Sabbaths and the new moons. See the account of the gates (4) in the explanation of the plan. <div eID="gen32560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32561" type="x-p"/> This verse has been adduced by the Roman Catholics to prove the perpetual virginity of the mother of our Lord; and it may be allowed to be as much to the purpose as any other that has been brought to prove this very precarious point, on which no stress should ever be laid by any man. Mary was a virgin when she brought forth Jesus.
entries.7147bdc9d52bc7ebd292447bd6327444ab83da0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32562" type="x-p"/> Mark well, and behold - Take notice of every thing; register all so fully that thou shalt be able to give the most minute information to the children of Israel.
entries.7af4791f6d6909fa0f28c7ff1e1aadd85c600f5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen32562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32563" type="x-p"/> The fat and the blood - These never went into common use; they were wholly offered to God. The blood was poured out; the fat consumed. <div eID="gen32563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32564" type="x-p"/> Because of all your abominations - Several MSS. of Kennicott's and De Rossi's read their abominations, referring to the strangers mentioned before.
entries.4884367a13d4ef50ffc4525b9fc0494cab5821a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen32564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32565" type="x-p"/> And the Levites that are gone away far from me - This refers to the schism of Jeroboam, who, when he set up a new worship, got as many of the priests and Levites to join him in his idolatry as he could. These, on the return from the captivity, should not be permitted to perform the functions of priests in the new temple; but they might be continued as keepers of all the charge of the house - be treasurers, guards of the temple, porters, etc.; see <reference osisRef="Eze.44.11-Eze.44.15">Eze 44:11-15</reference>. The whole of these passages refer to the period of time when the second temple was built.
entries.b57ef1f519e22b9e101a33bb6a409a5a8a1b9390: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen32565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32566" type="x-p"/> Come near to my table - To place the shew-bread there, and to burn incense on the golden altar in the holy of holies.
entries.f5aea9023e8ec1cf18511e81a7a63b8982ee17a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32567" type="x-p"/> No wool shall come upon them - The reason is plain; wool is more apt than linen to contract dirt and breed insects; linen breeds none; besides, this is a vegetable, and the other an animal substance. It was an ancient maxim, that whatever was taken from a dead body was impure in matters of religion, and should not be permitted to enter into the temple. The Egyptian priests always wore linen on their bodies, and shoes of matting or rushes on their feet. The Mohammedans never write the Koran upon vellum or skin of any kind, as they would consider that as a defilement.
entries.370cc86e21261a6f2ee39bdf87b6d7496bfd9ff7: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen32567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32568" type="x-p"/> Neither shall they shave their heads - The priests of Isis shaved their heads close to the skin; the priests of Budhoo do so still, their ordinances oblige them to shave their heads every tenth day. To let the hair grow long would have been improper; therefore the Lord commands them to poll - cut the hair short, but not to shave.
entries.353f98c17cedb877fe3403fab4bd009224b1f4ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen32568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32569" type="x-p"/> Neither shall they take for their wives a widow - This was prohibited to the high priest only, by Moses, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.13">Lev 21:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.14">Lev 21:14</reference>.
entries.4447a0d8271bf3bf15c56c19697bf070bbe8c5a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen32569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32570" type="x-p"/> And they shall come at no dead person to defile themselves - Touching the dead defiles a Hindoo now, as it formerly did a Jew; and they must bathe to become clean again.
entries.bd5b04103eeebc08b88d1dd948fc844502651cde: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen32570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32571" type="x-p"/> I am their inheritance - Those who affect to form their ecclesiastical matters on the model of the Jewish Church have with one consent left this out of the question. They will not live on the free-will offerings of the people; but must have vast revenues, and these secured to them by law. That every minister of God should be supported by the altar I grant; but I think, instead of that method of paying the parochial clergy which I see is so much objected to, and breeds so much dissension between the pastors and their flocks, it would be better, on these accounts, to assign them a portion of land adequate to their supply, or let the state maintain them as it does its other officers. In Israel God was their inheritance and their possession; but they had the breast and shoulder of all sin-offerings and trespass-offerings, and all dedicated things were theirs; and they had a portion of all the dough that was prepared for bread. These were considered as the Lord's property, and these he gave to them; and this is always implied in the Lord's being their inheritance and their possession. They had a plentiful support. <div eID="gen32571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32572" type="x-p"/> Hitherto tithes have been thought the best mode of paying the clergy, and providing for the poor of each parish; but these matters have undergone such alterations since the time of their institution, that some emendation of the system is at present absolutely necessary. <div eID="gen32572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32573" type="x-p"/> There should be a public acknowledgment of God in every nation, and this should be provided for by the state in a way the least burdensome to the people, that all may rejoice in the benefit. Happy the nations that have a Bible so correct, and a Liturgy so pure, as those in the British empire! In such cases, a religion established by the state is an unutterable blessing to the nation; only keep it to the Bible, and to the Liturgy, and all, under God, will be well; but when the sermon is against these, all is bad.  <chapter eID="Ezek.44"/> <div eID="gen32573" type="x-p"/>

entries.2281d8843cf8d33785194818750f2566d0a69759: <div eID="gen15319" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Position of the Different Classes of the People in Relation to the New Sanctuary</title> <div sID="gen15320" type="x-p"/> With the consecration of the altar of burnt-offering the way is opened for the congregation of Israel to appear in the sanctuary before the Lord, to serve Him with sacrifices. If, however, the use of the new house of God was to be in harmony with the holiness of the God who dwelt therein, it was requisite that still further directions should be given concerning the entering of the people into it, and the character of the servants of both the altar and the sanctuary. These directions follow in the chapter before us-first, as to the place which the prince was to occupy at the service in the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.1-Ezek.44.3">Eze 44:1-3</reference>); secondly, as to the admission of foreigners and the appointment of Levites and priests for the service (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.4-Ezek.44.16">Eze 44:4-16</reference>); and lastly, as to the conditions requisite for the administration of the priest’s office, and the duties and privileges of that office (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.17-Ezek.44.31">Eze 44:17-31</reference>). <div eID="gen15320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15321" type="x-p"/> The Place of the Prince in the Sanctuary. - Eze 44:1. <hi type="italic">And he brought me back by the way to the outer gate of the sanctuary, which looked toward the east; and it was shut.</hi> Eze 44:2. <hi type="italic">And Jehovah said to me, This gate shall be shut, shall not be opened, and no one shall enter thereby; because Jehovah, the God of Israel, has entered by it, it shall be shut.</hi> Eze 44:3. <hi type="italic">As for the prince, as prince he shall sit therein, to eat bread before Jehovah; from the way to the porch of the gate shall he go in, and from its way shall he go out.</hi> - From the inner court where Ezekiel had received the measurements of the altar of burnt-offering and the instructions concerning its consecration (Eze 43:5.), he is taken back to the east gate of the outer court, and finds this gate, which formed the principle entrance to the temple, closed. Jehovah explains this fact to him through the angel (ויּאמר is to be understood according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.6">Eze 43:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference>) thus: “this gate is to be shut, because Jehovah, the God of Israel, has entered into the temple thereby,” as we have already learned from Eze 43:2. Only the prince, as prince, was allowed to sit in it for the purpose of holding sacrificial meals there. So far the meaning of the words is clear and indisputable. For there can be no doubt whatever that <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.3">Eze 44:3</reference> introduces a more precise statement concerning the closing of the gate; in other words, that the right of sitting in the gate to eat bread before Jehovah, which is conceded to the priest, is intended as an explanation, <hi type="italic">resp</hi>. modification and limitation, of the statement והיה  (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.2">Eze 44:2</reference>). On the other hand, the more precise definition of the prerogative granted to the prince in <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.3">Eze 44:3</reference> is not quite clear, and therefore open to dispute. Such a prerogative is already indicated in the prominence expressly given to the prince, consisting partly in the fact that  את־הנּשׂיא is written first in an absolute form, and partly in the expression נשׂיא הוּא, which is repeated in the form of a circumstantial clause, “prince is he,” equivalent to “because he is prince, he is to sit there.” נשׂיא is neither the high priest, as many of the older commentators supposed, nor a collective term for the civil authorities of the people of Israel in the Messianic times (Hävernick), but the David who will be prince in Israel at that time, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23-Ezek.34.24">Eze 34:23-24</reference>, and Eze 37:24. “To eat bread before Jehovah” signifies to hold a sacrificial meal at the place of the divine presence, i.e., in the temple court, and is not to be restricted, as Kliefoth supposes, to that sacrificial meal “which was held after and along with the bloodless sacrifices, viz., the <hi type="italic">minchoth</hi>, and the shew-breads, and the sweet loaves of the Passover.” There is no authority in the usage of the language for this literal interpretation of the expression “to eat bread,” for אכל לחם means in general to partake of a meal, compare <reference osisRef="Gen.31.54">Gen 31:54</reference>, etc., and especially <reference osisRef="Exod.18.12">Exo 18:12</reference>, where Jethro “eats bread before God” with Aaron and the elders of Israel, that is to say, joins in a sacrificial meal composed of זבחים or slain-offerings. According to this view, which is the only one supported by usage, the prerogative secured to the נשׂיא of the future is not “that of participating in the sacrificial meals (of the priests), which were to be held daily with the <hi type="italic">minchoth</hi> and shew-bread, in opposition to the law which prevailed before” (Kliefoth), but simply that of holding his sacrificial meals in the gate, i.e., in the porch of the gate, whereas the people were only allowed to hold them in the court, namely, in the vicinity of the sacrificial kitchens. <div eID="gen15321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15322" type="x-p"/> There is also a difference of opinion concerning the meaning of the second statement in <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.3">Eze 44:3</reference> : “from the way of the porch of the gate shall he enter in, and thence shall he go out.” The suffix in מדּרכּו can only refer to אוּלם, “from the way from which he came (entered), from this way shall he go out again.” Hitzig follows the Rabbins, who understand the passage thus: “as the gate is to remain shut, he must go by the way to the porch which is directed inwardly, toward the court (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.9">Eze 40:9</reference>). He must have gone into the outer court through the north or the south gate, and by the way by which he came he also went back again.” But Kliefoth argues, in objection to this, that “if the prince was to eat the bread in the porch, the entrance through the south or the north gate would be of no use to him at all; as the gate which could be shut was at that door of the porch which was turned toward the outer court.” Moreover, he affirms that it is not at all the meaning of the text that he was to eat the bread in the porch, but that he was to eat it in the gate-building, and he was to come thither מדּרך אוּלם השּׁער, i.e., “from the place which served as a way to the gate porch, that is to say, the walk from the eastern entrance of the gate-building to the front of the porch, and from that was he to go out again.” The prince, therefore, was “to go into the gate-building as far as the front of the porch through the eastern entrance, there to eat his bread before Jehovah, and to come out again from thence, so that the gate at the western side of the gate porch still remained shut.” But we cannot regard either of these views as correct. There is no firm foundation in the text for Kliefoth’s assertion, that he was not to eat the bread in the porch, but in the gate-building. It is true that the porch is not expressly mentioned as the place where the eating was to take place, but simply the gate (בּו); yet the porch belonged to the gate as an integral part of the gate-building; and if דּרך אוּלם is the way to the porch, or the way leading to the porch, the words, “by the way to the porch shall he enter in,” imply clearly enough that he was to go into the porch and to eat bread there. This is also demanded by the circumstance, as the meaning of the words cannot possibly be that the prince was to hold his sacrificial meal upon the threshold of the gate, or in one of the guard-rooms, or in the middle of the gateway; and apart from the porch, there were no other places in the gate-building than those we have named. And again, the statement that the gate on the western side of the gate porch was to be shut, and not that against the eastern wall, is also destitute of proof, as דּרך אוּלם, the way to the porch, is not equivalent to the way “up to the front of the porch.” And if the prince was to hold the sacrificial meal behind the inner gate, which was closed, how was the food when it was prepared to be carried into the gate-building? Through a door of one of the guard-rooms? Such a supposition is hardly reconcilable with the significance of a holy sacrificial meal. In fact, it is a question whether eating in the gate-building with the inner door closed, so that it was not even possible to look toward the sanctuary, in which Jehovah was enthroned, could be called eating לפני. <div eID="gen15322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15323" type="x-p"/> Hitzig’s explanation of the words is not exposed to any of these difficulties, but it is beset by others. At the outset it is chargeable with improbability, as it is impossible to see any just ground why the prince, if he was to hold the sacrificial meal in the porch of the east gate, should not have been allowed to enter through this gate, but was obliged to take the circuitous route through the south or the north gate. Again, it is irreconcilable with the analogous statements in Ezekiel 46. According to Eze 46:1., the east gate of the inner court was to be shut, namely, during the six working days; but on the Sabbath and on the new moon it was to be opened. Then the prince was to come by the way of the gate porch from without, and during the preparation of his sacrifice by the priests to stand upon the threshold of the gate and worship. This same thing was to take place when the prince desired to offer a freewill offering on any of the week-days. The east gate was to be opened for him to this end; but after the conclusion of the offering of sacrifice it was to be closed again, whereas on the Sabbaths and new moons it was to stand open till the evening (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.12">Eze 46:12</reference> compared with <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.2">Eze 44:2</reference>). It is still further enjoined, that when offering these sacrifices the prince is to enter by the way of the gate porch, and to go out again by the same way (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.2">Eze 44:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.8">Eze 44:8</reference>); whereas on the feast days, on which the people appear before Jehovah, every one who comes, the priest along with the rest, is to go in and out through the north or the south gate (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.9">Eze 44:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.10">Eze 44:10</reference>). If, therefore, on the feast days, when the people appeared before Jehovah, the prince was to go into the temple in the midst of the people through the north or the south gate to worship, whereas on the Sabbaths and new moons, on which the people were not required to appear before the Lord, so that the prince alone had to bring the offerings for himself and the people, he was to enter by the way of the porch of the east gate, and to go out again by the same, and during the ceremony of offering the sacrifice was to stand upon the threshold of the inner east gate, it is obvious that the going in and out by the way of the porch of the gate was to take place by a different way from that through the north or the south gate. This other way could only be through the east gate, as no fourth gate existed. - The conclusion to which this brings us, so far as the passage before us is concerned, is that the shutting of the east gate of the outer court was to be the rule, but that there were certain exceptions which are not fully explained till Ezekiel 46, though they are hinted at in the chapter before us in the directions given there, that the prince was to hold the sacrificial meal in this gate. - The outer east gate, which was probably the one chiefly used by the people when appearing before the Lord in the earlier temple, both for going in and coming out, is to be shut in the new temple, and not to be made use of by the people for either entrance or exit, because the glory of the Lord entered into the temple thereby. This reason is of course not to be understood in the way suggested by the Rabbins, namely, that the departure of the Shechinah from the temple was to be prevented by the closing of the gate; but the thought is this: because this gateway had been rendered holy through the entrance of the Shechinah into the temple thereby, it was not to remain open to the people, so as to be desecrated, but was to be kept perpetually holy. This keeping holy was not prejudiced in any way by the fact that the prince held the sacrificial meal in the gate, and also entered the court through this gateway for the purpose of offering his sacrifice, which was made ready by the priests before the inner gate, and then was present at the offering of the sacrifice upon the altar, standing upon the threshold of the inner gate-building. דּרך אוּלם  is therefore the way which led from the outer flight of steps across the threshold past the guard-rooms to the gate porch at the inner end of the gate-building. By this way the priest was to go into the gate opened for him, and hold the sacrificial meal therein, namely, in the porch of this gate. That the offering of the sacrifice necessarily preceded the meal is assumed as self-evident, and the law of sacrifice in Ezekiel 46 first prescribes the manner in which the prince was to behave when offering the sacrifice, and how near to the altar he was to be allowed to go.
entries.8064d72cacd3c9c0b62d9435a6c0bead42655fef: <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.4-Ezek.44.16">Eze 44:4-16</reference> <div eID="gen15323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15324" type="x-p"/> The Position of Foreigners, Levites, and Priests in Relation to the Temple and the Temple Service. - The further precepts concerning the approach to the sanctuary, and the worship to be presented there, are introduced with a fresh exhortation to observe with exactness all the statutes and laws, in order that the desecration of the sanctuary which had formerly taken place might not be repeated, and are delivered to the prophet at the north gate in front of the manifestation of the glory of God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.4-Ezek.44.8">Eze 44:4-8</reference>). - Eze 44:4. <hi type="italic">And he brought me by the way of the north gate to the front of the house; and I looked, and behold the glory of Jehovah filled the house of Jehovah, and I fell down upon my face.</hi> Eze 44:5. <hi type="italic">And Jehovah said to me, Son of man, direct thy heart and see with thine eyes and hear with thine ears all that I say to thee with regard to all the statutes of the house of Jehovah and all its laws, and direct thy heart to the entering into the house through all the exits of the house,</hi> Eze 44:6. <hi type="italic">And say to the rebellious one, to the family of Israel, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Let it be sufficient for you, of all your abominations, O house of Israel,</hi> Eze 44:7. <hi type="italic">In that ye brought in foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary, to desecrate it, my house, when ye offered my food, fat and blood, and so they broke my covenant to all your abominations,</hi> Eze 44:8. <hi type="italic">And so ye did not keep the charge of my holy things, but made them keepers of my charge for you in my sanctuary.</hi> - From the outer gate to which Ezekiel had been taken, simply that he might be instructed concerning the entering thereby, he is once more conducted, after this has been done, by the way of the north gate to the front of the temple house, to receive the further directions there for the performance of the worship of God in the new sanctuary. The question, whether we are to understand by the north gate that of the outer or that of the inner court, cannot be answered with certainty. Hitzig has decided in favour of the latter, Kliefoth in favour of the former. The place to which he is conducted is אל־פּני הבּית, <hi type="italic">ad faciem domus</hi>, before the temple house, so that he had it before his eyes, i.e., was able to see it. As the gateway of the inner court was eight steps, about four cubits, higher than the outer court gate, this was hardly possible if he stood at or within the latter. הבּית, i.e., the temple house, could only be distinctly seen from the inner north gate. And the remark that it is more natural to think of the outer north gate, because the next thing said to the prophet has reference to the question who is to go into and out of the sanctuary, has not much force, as the instructions do not refer to the going in and out alone, but chiefly to the charge of Jehovah, i.e., to the maintenance of divine worship. <div eID="gen15324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15325" type="x-p"/> At the fresh standing-place the glory of the Lord, which filled the temple, met the sight of the prophet again, so that he fell down and worshipped once more (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.3">Eze 43:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.5">Eze 43:5</reference>). This remark is not intended “to indicate that now, after the preliminary observations in Ezekiel 43:13-44:3, the true <hi type="italic">thorah</hi> commences” (Kliefoth), but to show the unapproachable glory and holiness of the new temple. For <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.5">Eze 44:5</reference>, see <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.4">Eze 40:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.11">Eze 43:11</reference>-12. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.6">Eze 44:6</reference> אל־מרי is placed at the head in a substantive form for the sake of emphasis, and בּית־ישׂראל is appended in the form of an apposition. For the fact itself, see Eze 2:8. רב־לּכם followed by מן, a sufficiency of anything, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.9.28">Exo 9:28</reference>; 1Ki 12:28, is equivalent to “there is enough for you to desist from it.” The תּועבות, from which they are to desist, are more precisely defined in Eze 44:6. They consisted in the fact that the Israelites admitted foreigners, heathen, uncircumcised in heart and flesh, into the sanctuary, to desecrate it during the offering of sacrifice. It is not expressly stated, indeed, that they admitted uncircumcised heathen to the offering of sacrifice, but this is implied in what is affirmed. The offering of sacrifice in the temple of Jehovah is not only permitted in the Mosaic law to foreigners living in Israel, but to some extent prescribed (<reference osisRef="Lev.17.10">Lev 17:10</reference>,<reference osisRef="Lev.17.12">Lev 17:12</reference>; Num 15:13.). It was only in the paschal meal that no 'בן was allowed to participate (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.43">Exo 12:43</reference>). To do this, he must first of all be circumcised (v. 44). Solomon accordingly prays to the Lord in his temple-prayer that He will also hearken to the prayer of the foreigner, who may come from a distant land for the Lord’s name sake to worship in His house (1Ki 8:41.). The reproof in the verse before us is apparently at variance with this. Raschi would therefore understand by בּני־נכר, Israelites who had fallen into heathen idolatry. Rosenmüller, on the other hand, is of opinion that the Israelites were blamed because they had accepted <hi type="italic">victimas et libamina</hi> from the heathen, and offered them in the temple, which had been prohibited in Lev 25:22. Hävernick understands by the sons of the foreigner, Levites who had become apostates from Jehovah, and were therefore placed by Ezekiel on a par with the idolatrous sons of the foreigner. And lastly, Hitzig imagines that they were foreign traders, who had been admitted within the sacred precincts as sellers of sacrificial animals, incense, and so forth. All these are alike arbitrary and erroneous. The apparent discrepancy vanishes, if we consider the more precise definition of בּני , viz., “uncircumcised in heart and flesh.” Their being uncircumcised in heart is placed first, for the purpose of characterizing the foreigners as godless heathen, who ere destitute not only of the uncircumcision of their flesh, but also of that of the heart, i.e., of piety of heart, which Solomon mentions in his prayer as the motive for the coming of distant strangers to the temple. By the admission of such foreigners as these, who had no fear of God at all, into the temple during the sacrificial worship, Israel had defiled the sanctuary. את־בּיתי is in apposition to the suffix to חלּלו. The food of Jehovah (לחמי) is sacrifice, according to <reference osisRef="Lev.3.11">Lev 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.21.6">Lev 21:6</reference>, etc., and is therefore explained by “fat and blood.” ויּפרוּ, which the lxx changed in an arbitrary manner into the second person, refers to the “foreigners,” the heathen. By their treading the temple in their ungodliness they broke the covenant of the Lord with His people, who allowed this desecration of His sanctuary. אל כּל־תּועבות, in addition to all your abominations. How grievous a sin was involved in this is stated in Eze 44:8. The people of Israel, by their unrighteous admission of godless heathen into the temple, not only failed to show the proper reverence for the holy things of the Lord, but even made these heathen, so to speak, servants of God for themselves in His sanctuary. These last words are not to be understood literally, but spiritually. Allowing them to tread the temple is regarded as equivalent to appointing them to take charge of the worship in the temple. For שׁמר , see <reference osisRef="Lev.18.30">Lev 18:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.22.9">Lev 22:9</reference>, and the commentary on Lev 8:35. <div eID="gen15325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15326" type="x-p"/> The Lord would guard against such desecration of His sanctuary in the future. To this end the following precepts concerning the worship in the new temple are given. - Eze 44:9. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall come into my sanctuary, of all the foreigners that are in the midst of the sons of Israel;</hi> Eze 44:10. <hi type="italic">But even the Levites, who have gone away from me in the wandering of Israel, which wandered away from me after its idols, they shall bear their guilt.</hi> Eze 44:11. <hi type="italic">They shall be servants in my sanctuary, as guards at the gates of the house and serving in the house; they shall slay the burnt-offering and the slain-offering for the people, and shall stand before it to serve them.</hi> Eze 44:12. <hi type="italic">Because they served them before their idols, and became to the house of Israel a stumbling-block to guilt, therefore I have lifted my hand against them, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah, that they should bear their guilt.</hi> Eze 44:13. <hi type="italic">They shall not draw near to me to serve me as priests, and to draw near to all my holy things, to the most holy, but shall bear their disgrace and all their abominations which they have done.</hi> Eze 44:14. <hi type="italic">And so will I make them guards of the charge of the house with regard to all its service, and to all that is performed therein.</hi> Eze 44:15. <hi type="italic">But the priests of the tribe of Levi, the sons of Zadok, who have kept the charge of my sanctuary on the wandering of the sons of Israel from me, they shall draw near to me to serve me, and stand before me, offer to me fat and blood, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> Eze 44:16. <hi type="italic">They shall come into my sanctuary, and they draw near to my table to serve me, and shall keep my charge.</hi> - In order that all desecration may be kept at a distance from the new sanctuary, foreigners uncircumcised in heart and flesh are not to be admitted into it; and even of the Levites appointed for the service of the sanctuary according to the Mosaic law, all who took part in the falling away of the people into idolatry are to be excluded from investiture with the priests’ office as a punishment for their departure from the Lord, and only to be allowed to perform subordinate duties in connection with the worship of God. On the other hand, the descendants of Zadok, who kept themselves free from all straying into idolatry, are to perform the specifically priestly service at the altar and in the sanctuary, and they alone. The meaning and design of the command, to shut out the foreigners uncircumcised in heart from all access to the sanctuary, are not that the intermediate position and class of foreigners living in Israel should henceforth be abolished (Kliefoth); for this would be at variance with <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.22">Eze 47:22</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.23">Eze 47:23</reference>, according to which the foreigners (גּרים) were to receive a possession of their own in the fresh distribution of the land, which not only presupposes their continuance within the congregation of Israel, but also secures it for the time to come. The meaning is rather this: No heathen uncircumcised in heart, i.e., estranged in life from God, shall have access to the altar in the new sanctuary. The emphasis of the prohibition lies here, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.7">Eze 44:7</reference>, upon their being uncircumcised in heart; and the reason for the exclusion of foreigners consists not so much in the foreskin of the flesh as in the spiritual foreskin, so that not only the uncircumcised heathen, but also Israelites who were circumcised in flesh, were to keep at a distance from the sanctuary if they failed to possess circumcision of heart. The ל before  כּל־בּן  serves the purpose of comprehension, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.9.10">Gen 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.11.42">Lev 11:42</reference>, etc. (compare <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §310 <hi type="italic">a</hi>). Not only are foreigners who are estranged from God to be prevented from coming into the sanctuary, but even the Levites, who fell into idolatry at the time of the apostasy of the Israelites, are to bear their guilt, i.e., are to be punished for it by exclusion from the rights of the priesthood.
